blocks.raw: <Tip>When a question specifies a material by common Filipino name (kawayan, coco lumber, nipa) and asks about structural suitability, first identify the material's applicable standard or non-code status. If the material lacks ASTM or ISO standardization, check whether DPWH case-by-case approval is noted or if it is limited to non-structural use. Many vernacular materials are excellent for infill, interior applications, and secondary structural members but unsuitable for primary seismic resisting systems without additional testing and engineer approval.</Tip>

blocks.raw: <WikiMistakeCard title="Confusing Bamboo Species and Structural Capacity" severity="critical">Candidates often state that all bamboo has identical structural properties. In reality, Kawayan tinik (Dendrocalamus asper) and Bayog (Bambusa blumeana) have different allowable stress values per ISO 22157 testing. Kawayan tinik typically allows higher bending stress (8-10 MPa) than Bayog (6-7 MPa) due to denser culm structure. Material testing is required to establish species-specific properties; candidates must not assume interchangeability.</WikiMistakeCard>

blocks.raw: <WikiMistakeCard title="Assuming Coco Lumber Requires No Quality Control" severity="high">Candidates sometimes specify coco lumber as a sustainable choice without verifying FPRDI grading documentation or preservation application. DPWH acceptance requires graded lumber with copper-based fungicide preservation and documented 10-12 year service life. Using ungraded or untreated coco lumber violates DPWH specifications and voids material acceptance on public works projects.</WikiMistakeCard>

blocks.raw: <WikiMistakeCard title="Overestimating Adobe and Nipa in Seismic Regions" severity="critical">Adobe blocks (1-3 MPa compressive strength) and nipa palm thatching are marketed as sustainable but are unsuitable for primary structural members in earthquake-prone Philippines. Candidates must recognize that while these materials work in vernacular low-seismic-risk contexts, they do not meet National Building Code requirements for lateral load resistance. Adobe may be used only for non-structural infill or cladding with reinforced concrete backing.</WikiMistakeCard>

blocks.raw:
• Specifying vernacular materials for primary structural systems without checking ISO 22156 height/storey limitations (max 7 m, 2 storeys for bamboo)
  • Assuming non-standardized materials (rattan, abaca composites) meet structural code without DPWH engineer approval documentation
  • Forgetting that coco lumber preservation (fungicide) must be verified and durability tested for the intended service environment
  • Confusing lower embodied carbon with lower total lifecycle cost; vernacular materials often have higher maintenance costs offsetting material savings
  • Specifying nipa palm or rattan without recognizing they are non-structural or maintenance-intensive (annual inspection, 15-20 year replacement cycle)
  • Using vernacular materials in high-moisture or corrosive environments (coastal salt spray, industrial areas) without durability verification
